newsitem.title: USA: ISSUER FOCUS - Milwaukee ballpark bonds go to market.
newsitem.headline: ISSUER FOCUS - Milwaukee ballpark bonds go to market.

text.p: A bond issue for a new ballpark for the Milwaukee Brewers American League baseball team heads to market Wednesday under a cloud of controversy that continues to hang over the project.
A group led by Bear, Stearns & Co is scheduled to price $146.7 million of tax-exempt sales tax revenue bonds for the Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District.

The MBIA Insurance Corp-insured deal is a remarketing of convertible option bonds, secured by a guarenteed investment contract, the district quietly sold in December. Those bonds will be remarketed to long-term, fixed-rate debt backed by revenues from a 0.1 percent sales tax collected in five southeast Wisconsin counties.

The legality of that tax is being challenged by a group of Milwaukee area taxpayers, who have turned to the U.S. Court of Appeals in Chicago after a U.S. District Court judge in Milwaukee dismissed the case on the basis the constitutionality of the tax had been upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
Attorneys for the district have issued opinions the federal lawsuit has no merit.

But plaintiffs and their lawyer have contended that they have a strong basis for appeal and expect to have a "fairer" hearing of their lawsuit outside of Wisconsin. The federal appeals court has yet to set a date to hear the appeal.
"We still feel we have a really good chance," said Bob Collison, head of the Libertarian Party of Metro Milwaukee, one of the plaintiffs in the case.
Collison said the district was trying to push the project to the point of no return so that no matter what happens, the stadium would have to be completed.
Another controversy has arisen over the cost of the 42,500-seat, convertible-roofed stadium and the district's responsibility for any costs over the $250 million initial budget.

In fact, State Sen. Joe Wineke, D-Verona, introduced a bill Monday that limits the district's bond issuance to $160 million and prohibits any sales tax revenues from being used for lease payments for other stadium costs.
The preliminary official statement for the bond issue states that the district may issue another $45 million of parity bonds for stadium equipment.

Wineke has said the aim of his bill is to make the Brewers pay for cost overruns. The possibility of legislation is mentioned in the bond prospectus, which said the district believes such a move "would impair the district's contractual committments to build the stadium and the district's ability to fund the project in accordance with the preliminary budget."
The document also states that a first lien on sales tax revenues for debt service on the bonds would not be affected by a failure to complete the stadium.
Mike Morgan, a spokesman for the district, said Tuesday that district officials were formulating a reponse to the public and to lawmakers about cost overruns.
Underwriters for the deal reported receiving some questions about the controversies.
"Anytime you do a stadium financing there's going to be controversy," said Dan Keating, a senior managing director at Bear Stearns. "But it seems to have died out from the marketing side."
He pointed out that in addition to MBIA insurance, the deal earned underlying ratings of A3 from Moody's Investors Service and A-minus from Standard & Poor's Corp.
A retail order period began Tuesday with Milwaukee-based Robert W. Baird & Co, the co-senior manager on the deal, promoting the deal's double tax-exemption for Wisconsin residents.
Keating said he also expected interest in the bonds from the "usual cast" of institutions.
The structure for the deal shows $56.3 million of serial bonds carrying maturites from 1998 to 2017, $33.9 million of term bonds due in 2021 and $56.5 million of term bonds due in 2026.
The district will co-own the stadium with the Brewers, which had intially pledged to finance $90 million of the project.

The team's inability to secure a bond-financed loan from a state bonding agency for a portion of that committment led to a new plan that provided $50 million in loans from the city of Milwaukee and other parties.
Another $40 million is expected to be raised from the sale of naming rights to Miller Brewing Co., upfront concession payments and a letter of credit from the American League.
The state and the county and city of Milwaukee have also committed to pay $72 million in infrastructure costs for the project.
